source: Choudhury et al. (2026, ICLR) BED-LLM: Intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design
finding: Choosing each yes/no question by explicit expected information gain (EIG), with code doing the maths, beats just prompting the model to ask a good question in 20 Questions.
numbers: Average gain +37.4 percentage points over direct prompting across models and target sets; success more than doubled in over half of setups and never fell. GPT-4o Animals 45% -> 93%; Mistral-Large Celebrities 19% -> 91%; Llama-3.1-8B Things 10% -> 26%. 100 targets per set, 6 LLMs, 3 sets.
limits: Target space is open: the questioner is not told the list of entities.
agent_relevance: Strong case that the code, not the model, should compute which test separates the hypotheses.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026, ICLR) BED-LLM: Intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design
finding: Asking the model to pick the best question itself ('implicit maximization') over the same candidate questions works much worse than computing EIG in code.
numbers: Table 1 Animals: GPT-4o BED-LLM 93% vs implicit max 70%; Mistral-Large 95% vs 53%; Qwen2.5-72B 95% vs 61%. Implicit max still beat Prompt-Only (GPT-4o 70 vs 45).
limits: Same candidate questions and filtered hypotheses for both arms.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model judge 'most informative'. Judging is a weaker substitute for arithmetic.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026, ICLR) BED-LLM: Intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design
finding: Keeping beliefs by in-context learning alone fails; sampling hypotheses and filtering them against the answer history is what makes EIG work.
numbers: Ablation 'ICL Beliefs' (no filtering): Animals GPT-4o 25% vs BED-LLM 93%; Qwen2.5-72B 46% vs 95%; Mistral-Large 53% vs 95%.
limits: Authors say raw in-context beliefs are often incoherent.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis set must be kept by code and pruned by every observed answer (fits G2/G3 in the schema).

source: Choudhury et al. (2026, ICLR) BED-LLM: Intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design
finding: True EIG (with a noisy likelihood) beats the plain 'split the hypotheses evenly' rule (Split baseline) by a smaller margin than it beats prompting.
numbers: Animals GPT-4o: BED-LLM 93, Entropy 88, Split 83. Celebrities Mistral-Large: 91 vs 68 vs 63. Things GPT-4o: 64 vs 49 vs 40. Authors: benefit comes mainly from targeting the proper EIG, not from the entropy term.
limits: Split uses a deterministic likelihood; Entropy uses BED-LLM's likelihood.
agent_relevance: A simple even-split rule gets much of the gain; full EIG adds a further step. Start with the split rule.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026, ICLR) BED-LLM: Intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design
finding: Measuring uncertainty in answer space beats measuring it in hypothesis space (prior-likelihood vs data-estimation pairing).
numbers: Data-Estimation ablation Animals GPT-4o 70% vs BED-LLM 93%; Data-Estimation also ran over 10x slower (1d 17h vs about 2.5h for Qwen2.5-72B on the Animals set).
limits: Runtime is wall-clock for the whole Animals set.
agent_relevance: Estimate EIG over the small space of test outcomes, not over free-text hypotheses.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026, ICLR) BED-LLM: Intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design
finding: The gain survives a mismatch between the questioner's model of answers and the real answerer, and carries over to movie preference elicitation.
numbers: Questioner and answerer were different LLMs (for example Q Qwen2.5-72B, A GPT-4o-mini) and BED-LLM still led. Movie task: mean rating of 10 recommendations, 200 users, 5 turns; BED-LLM shown above Prompt-Only and Entropy in the figure (no exact table value read).
limits: Simulated users and answerers are LLMs, not people.
agent_relevance: Test selection stays useful when the world answers differently than the model predicts.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026, ICLR) BED-LLM: Intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design
finding: Cost of explicit EIG is modest if the likelihood calls are reused.
numbers: Wall-clock, Qwen2.5-72B Animals: BED-LLM 2h30m, Split 2h46m, Entropy 3h10m, Implicit Max 2h28m; Prompt-Only and CoT are the cheapest (about 26-45 min; row labels partly garbled in the extracted text).
limits: Table 3 row labels partly misaligned in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Roughly 4-6x the cost of one prompt per turn for roughly double the success.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov, Ellis (2023) Active preference inference using language models and probabilistic reasoning
finding: An early (2023) system chose questions by expected entropy reduction over product hypotheses scored by a prompted LLM; it asked more informative questions than a vanilla LLM or ReAct.
numbers: GPT-4 shopper task, 150 tasks, 10 products each, yes/no questions only, 8 proposed questions per turn. With binary reward the entropy-reduction LLM beat both baselines after more than one question; after 3 questions it beat the baselines after 4. Curve values only in figures.
limits: Simulated user is GPT-4; only yes/no; 10 products. At the last question vanilla got more info, but little was left.
agent_relevance: Early proof that proposing several candidate questions and ranking by expected entropy helps even with a prompted likelihood.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov, Ellis (2023) Active preference inference using language models and probabilistic reasoning
finding: Expected entropy minimisation and expected model change are the same objective in this setup.
numbers: Paper shows equivalence (appendix A.1) because the expected cross-entropy term is the same for all q, a.
limits: Holds under the paper's modelling assumptions.
agent_relevance: One scoring rule is enough; no need to build two.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs
finding: Uncertainty of Thoughts (UoT): simulate possible answers to each candidate question, score by information gain, pick best; success rises 38.1% on average over direct prompting.
numbers: 5 datasets (20Q Common, Thing; medical DX, MedDG; troubleshooting FloDial), 5 LLMs. Llama3-70B +46.6%; UoT beat CoT-SC by 33.8%, Reflexion by 29.9%, original ToT by 28.3%, adapted ToT by 12.4%. Llama3-70B 20Q Common closed-set 51.4 -> 55.9; DX closed-set 83.7 -> 90.4.
limits: Gains are small on some cells: Mistral-Large 20Q Thing closed set 13.0 -> 18.5. Answerer is GPT-4 (checked on 10% of dialogues).
agent_relevance: Tree search over simulated answers with an info-gain reward beats generic reasoning scaffolds for choosing queries.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs
finding: Removing the information-gain reward hurts; at matched token cost UoT still beats other test-time scaffolds.
numbers: About 9k GPT-4 tokens: UoT 20Q 54.4, MD 92.5, TB 66.0 vs adapted ToT depth 4: 40.9, 86.7, 63.7. About 4.6k tokens: CoT-SC (k=33) 32.6/37.6/42.5. Pruned UoT 48.1/88.4/63.2 at 4.7k.
limits: Simulation depth limited to 3 steps for cost.
agent_relevance: Even at equal compute the info-gain reward matters; a self-evaluation heuristic reward in ToT does worse.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT reached 97.0% success on simplified diagnosis (DX) with GPT-4 and cut conversation length to 2.0 questions.
numbers: DX GPT-4 UoT(CS) 97.0% success, mean successful conversation length 2.0 vs 3.0-3.5 for direct-prompting methods. MedDG: 88.0% GPT-4, 81.4% Gemini-1.5-Pro. Troubleshooting 43.7% -> 67.3%.
limits: DX is a simplified closed-set task with a fixed disease list.
agent_relevance: Diagnosis-like closed hypothesis sets are the best case for EIG.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025, ICLR) Active task disambiguation with LLMs
finding: Framing clarifying questions as Bayesian experimental design: choosing the question whose answers split the space of compatible solutions gives better disambiguation than reasoning only in question space.
numbers: Code tasks, after eliciting 4 test-case requirements. HumanEval GPT-3.5-turbo binary questions 70.8% (base) -> 85.6% (EIG); open questions 75.9 -> 85.0. Llama3-8B binary 53.0 -> 65.8, open 64.8 -> 75.5. 48 tasks, 3 run and 3 eval seeds.
limits: Gap shrinks for stronger models: GPT-4o-mini binary 79.6 -> 81.5 on HumanEval.
agent_relevance: Good for 'ask the user' steps: sample solutions, ask what splits them. Benefit is larger for weaker base models.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025, ICLR) Active task disambiguation with LLMs
finding: On the harder APPS code benchmark the EIG advantage is larger and holds for a stronger model.
numbers: APPS, 47 tasks, 4 questions: GPT-4o-mini binary 62.9 -> 75.3; open 75.1 -> 87.2. GPT-3.5 binary 62.4 -> 71.3; open 69.7 -> 77.3. Zero-shot GPT-4o-mini is only 35% on APPS vs 70% on HumanEval.
limits: Open questions are more informative but cost the human more effort to answer.
agent_relevance: Harder tasks leave more ambiguity to resolve, so EIG-chosen questions pay more.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025, ICLR) Active task disambiguation with LLMs
finding: On 20 Questions with animals, EIG over sampled solutions ranked best at most turns for GPT-3.5, but the edge over a plain implicit prompt is small or absent for a stronger model.
numbers: Average rank of target after t=10 questions (lower is better). GPT-3.5: EIG-uniform 6.2, EIG-logprobs 4.1, implicit-ToT 5.1, implicit 4.9. GPT-4o-mini: 6.8, 6.0, 6.6, 5.5 (implicit best).
limits: 15 animals, 5 run seeds; the metric is rank, not success rate.
agent_relevance: EIG is not always better than a plain implicit prompt on a strong model; check per model.

source: Zhang, Lu, Jaitly (2024) Probing the multi-turn planning capabilities of LLMs via 20 Question games
finding: Baseline: in 2023 even GPT-4 won only a third to a half of 20-question games; weaker models failed through early enumeration, redundancy and inconsistent questions.
numbers: Success: GPT-4 31% Things, 50% Celebrities; GPT-3.5 28%/27%; Claude-2 21%/31%; Vicuna 7B 9%/6%. GPT-4 used 17.8 and 17.3 turns of 20. 30 items x 5 runs. Judge error rate about 3%. Paper also says strong LLMs beat human players by a large margin.
limits: Success counts exact match to the entity.
agent_relevance: Pre-EIG baseline. Without code, models do not run a clean binary search.

source: Zhang, Lu, Jaitly (2024) Probing the multi-turn planning capabilities of LLMs via 20 Question games
finding: Training can raise informativeness: reinforcement learning from game play lifted a 7B model from 9% to 26% on Things; cloning only successful games helped, cloning all games did not.
numbers: Vicuna 7B Things success 0.09 -> V-RLGP 7B 0.26; 13B 0.18 -> 0.27. Behaviour cloning: all games 0.13, successes only 0.23 (7B).
limits: Training, not scaffold, so out of scope for our no-training agent.
agent_relevance: Shows the gap is learnable, but our route is code scaffolding.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to ask informative questions: preference optimization and expected information gain
finding: Preference-training a 7B model on pairs of high-EIG vs low-EIG questions raises question informativeness and success, even on new domains.
numbers: Llama-2-Chat 7B, 20Q with 8 candidates. INLG: zero-shot success 56.7%, EIG 0.34 -> DPO 68.9%, EIG 0.45. Things 51.1 -> 61.1 (EIG 0.29 -> 0.40). Celebrities 71.1 -> 72.2. Plain fine-tuning lowered success on all three sets (for example 56.7 -> 46.6).
limits: With 29 candidates (BigBench) success rose 17.2 -> 31.0 but EIG fell 0.31 -> 0.28; abstract targets stayed hard (7.7% -> 23.1%).
agent_relevance: Models can be taught EIG, but computing EIG here needs a closed candidate list.

source: Handa et al. (2024) Bayesian preference elicitation with language models (OPEN)
finding: OPEN framework: Bayesian experimental design chooses the question, the LM only words it and extracts features; this beat LM-only elicitation in a human study.
numbers: Scored by Time-Integrated Delta Accuracy (TIDA) across five question/prediction combinations; OPEN pairwise questions beat LM-only pairwise questions. LM open-ended questions beat pairwise when judged by an LM, but that gain is smaller than the benefit of OPEN's own prediction method. Exact TIDA values only in figures.
limits: Authors list open-ended questions compatible with OPEN prediction as future work.
agent_relevance: Division of labour matches our schema: code picks, model verbalises.

source: Wang, Zollo, Zemel, Namkoong (2025) Adaptive elicitation of latent information using natural language
finding: Meta-trained LM that simulates future answers to estimate EIG improves 20 Questions, opinion polling and student assessment; lookahead beats one-step EIG.
numbers: Three datasets, 10,000 simulated runs each, unseen entities. Greedy EIG beat base Llama-3.1-8B, in-context tuning and embedding-distance picks on accuracy and perplexity; MCTS planning beat greedy EIG in all cases and both beat random. Greedy EIG loses at most a constant fraction of the best achievable gain (Proposition 2).
limits: Needs meta-training of the simulator.
agent_relevance: Lookahead adds over one-step EIG but costs more compute.

source: Chan et al. (2025) Conformal information pursuit for interactively guiding LLMs
finding: LLM probability estimates are over- or under-confident, which damages entropy-based query choice; conformal prediction-set size is a more robust uncertainty signal.
numbers: 20 Questions and MediQ: C-IP gave better predictive performance and shorter query chains than Information Pursuit with raw or temperature-scaled probabilities. Coverage close to target at 1-alpha 0.99, under-coverage at lower targets in some settings.
limits: On MediQ, only competitive with single-turn prediction, not better.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the model's own probabilities as the EIG likelihood; use counts over sampled hypotheses.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Models often cannot identify the single needed question even when they can solve the full problem.
numbers: QuestBench: pick the right clarifying question among options. Logic-Q and Planning-Q about 40-50% at best (o1-preview ZS+CoT 49.9% and 42.3%); GSME-Q over 90% and GSM-Q 77-94% for most frontier models. Chain of thought and few-shot gave no consistent gain.
limits: Each task has exactly one missing variable, so choosing the question is simple in principle.
agent_relevance: The 'which input is missing' step should come from the constraint structure in code, not from asking the model.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation
finding: Related failure: in multi-turn underspecified tasks models guess early and do not recover.
numbers: Average drop of 39% across six generation tasks from single-turn to multi-turn; 200,000+ simulated conversations; loss is mostly reliability, little aptitude. LLMs make assumptions early and prematurely attempt final answers.
limits: Not an EIG paper; information arrives in shards rather than through model questions.
agent_relevance: Argues for not committing to an answer until a test settles the open hypotheses.

source: Yiu, Kosoy, Gopnik (2023) Imitation versus innovation: what children can do that LLMs cannot (yet)
finding: Children discover causal structure by acting on a blicket machine; LLMs given the children's data in text struggled.
numbers: Children aged 3-7 (n=42) and adults (n=30) on tool tasks: superficial match 88.4% vs 84.9%; functional innovation 85.2% children vs 95.7% adults; LLMs did well on the first, poorly on the second. On the blicket detector, LLMs, deep RL and behaviour cloning struggled to extract causal over-hypotheses (reported from Kosoy et al., in prep).
limits: Position paper; blicket results are summarised, not tabulated. Some models cited the published blicket papers (contamination).
agent_relevance: Sets the human benchmark: the child's own interventions are the evidence; text-only models do not use that loop.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 showed no sign of directed exploration, the value-of-information drive that EIG formalises.
numbers: Horizon task: no horizon effect in the unequal-information condition (beta = -0.15 +/- 0.27, z = -0.56, p = .58) while humans show it. It repeated options it had seen more often. GPT-3 also failed the intervention-vs-observation causal task.
limits: GPT-3 (2022) only; later models not tested here.
agent_relevance: Do not expect information seeking from the model by default; supply it from code.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 did well on vignette-based decisions from description, so failures are specific to active information search and intervention.
numbers: Mean regret over 13,000 problems (Peterson et al.) was low for davinci; several human biases reproduced. Causal-chain intervention inference matched neither humans nor the normative answer.
limits: Vignette tasks may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Competence on described tasks does not predict competence in active experimentation.
